The line $x=-4$ intersects the x-axis at point $C$ and intersects the parabola at point $D$. If the distances from points $B$, $D$, $C$ to the same line are $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_3$ respectively, is there a line $l$ such that $d_1=d_2=\frac{d_3}{2}$? If such a line exists, please directly write down the value of $d_3$; if it does not exist, please explain the reason.

$\therefore$ Point C ($-4,0$), Point B ($2,0$), Point D ($-4,-6$),

$\therefore OC=4$, $OB=2$, $CD=6$,

$\therefore \triangle CDB$ is an isosceles right triangle,

$\therefore CH=CD\cdot\sin 45^\circ=6\times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=3\sqrt{2}$,

$\because BD=2CH$,

$\therefore BD=6\sqrt{2}$,

$\because CO:OB=2:1$,

$\therefore$ The line $l_1$ passing through point O and parallel to BD satisfies the condition,

Draw line $BE\perp l_1$, $DF\perp l_1$ at point F, $CH$ intersects line $l_1$ at point G, outside $\triangle CDB$ draw line $l_2\parallel DB$, extending CH to intersect line $l_2$ at point G', making $CH=HG'$,

$\because BE=DF$, i.e., $d_1=d_2$,

$\therefore \frac{CG}{BE}=\frac{CO}{BO}=\frac{2}{1}$, $\frac{CG}{GH}=\frac{2}{1}$,

$\therefore \frac{d_3}{d_1}=\frac{2}{1}$,

$\therefore d_1=d_2=\frac{1}{2}d_3$,

$\therefore CG=\frac{2}{3}CH$,

$\therefore d_3=\frac{2}{3}\times 3\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}$;

$\therefore d_3=CG' =2CH=6\sqrt{2}$;

As shown in the diagram, through points H, O draw line $l_3$, draw $BE\perp l_3$ at point E, $DF\perp l_3$ at point F, $CG\perp l_3$ at point G, draw $HI\perp x$-axis at point I,

$\therefore DH=BH$, $BE=DF$, i.e., $d_1=d_2$,

$\because CO:OB=2:1$,

$\therefore d_1:d_2=\frac{d_3}{2}$,

$\therefore HI=CI=\frac{1}{2}CB=3$,

$\therefore OI=4−3=1$,

$\because BD=2CH$,

$\therefore BD=6\sqrt{2}$,

$\because CO:OB=2:1$,

$\therefore \frac{d_3}{d_1}=\frac{2}{1}$,

$\therefore d_1=d_2=\frac{1}{2}d_3$,

$\therefore CG=\frac{2}{3}CH$,

$\therefore d_3=\frac{2}{3}\times 3\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}$;
